passage: On his first day in the new office tower, Deepak spent two minutes walking the corridor to find both stairwells, then went back to his desk. Mahima, at the next desk, raised an eyebrow. "Fire inspector?" "Habit," he said. In July the city's official alert turned orange for heavy rain by evening. Deepak read it, looked at the clear sky, and packed up at three. In his backpack sat the same small pouch as always: a torch, a water bottle, a charged power bank, a folded plastic sheet. "The sky looks fine," Mahima said. "Everyone else is staying." "Then I'll look silly tomorrow," he said, smiling. The rain came, but lighter than forecast. Next morning Mahima grinned. "Your big escape?" "Worth it," Deepak said, and meant it. "I'd rather be teased than stuck on the flyover till midnight."

qa.q: What was in Deepak's pouch?
qa.a: A torch, a water bottle, a charged power bank and a folded plastic sheet.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel about being teased the next morning?
qa.a: Relaxed and unbothered 🙂 He said "Worth it" and meant it, because a little teasing mattered far less to him than being stuck on the flyover.

qa.q: Why was leaving at three a sound choice even though the rain came lighter than forecast?
qa.a: Deepak followed the official alert rather than the clear sky, and the cost of being wrong was only some teasing, much smaller than being stranded.

qa.q: How might Mahima come to see Deepak's habits?
qa.a: At first Mahima finds them funny, but seeing Deepak calmly accept looking silly may make Mahima wonder whether staying late in a storm alert was the wiser choice.

grounding: A young man notes exits, carries a small kit, and leaves on an official rain alert, accepting teasing over the risk of being stuck.

passage: "Dilnaz, get your charger. We're going to Khala's tonight." "Because of one SMS?" Dilnaz didn't move from the sofa. "Zeenat Aapa, the road is dry." "The dam is releasing water after midnight. The message says low-lying areas. That's us." "You said the same last year and nothing happened." "And we lost nothing." Zeenat pulled the go-bag down from the top of the cupboard: medicines, torch, copies of the papers, two water bottles. "Kit's ready. It takes us fifteen minutes." "The neighbours will laugh." "Let them. If the water doesn't come, you can make fun of me all week. I'll even buy the samosas." Dilnaz groaned but reached for her shoes. "Double samosas." "Deal. Lock the balcony door."

qa.q: What was in the go-bag?
qa.a: Medicines, a torch, copies of the papers and two water bottles.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz worried about, apart from the water?
qa.a: That the neighbours would laugh at them for leaving because of one SMS 😅

qa.q: Which earlier choice made leaving easy for Zeenat?
qa.a: Keeping the go-bag packed in the cupboard, so following the warning took fifteen minutes instead of a long scramble.

qa.q: What would change if Zeenat waited until the road was wet before leaving?
qa.a: By then the water might already be rising around the house, and the calm trip to Khala's could become a rushed and risky one.

grounding: A young woman follows an official dam-release message without waiting for proof, with a ready kit and a joke about being wrong.

passage: I'm Suraj, and I've made peace with being the uncool friend. Last month Wasim and I went to a crowded music night in an old hall. Before sitting down, I did my usual thing and found the two exits, one beside the stage and one behind the snack counter. Wasim laughed. Halfway through, the lights flickered and a burning smell drifted in. A staff member took the mic: "As a precaution, please make your way outside." Plenty of people stayed put, filming the stage. I didn't wait to see smoke. I tapped Wasim, said "Let's go," and walked to the counter exit. He followed, grumbling. It turned out to be a burnt fuse in the kitchen. We missed three songs, and Wasim teased me all the way home. My face went warm, sure. But a warm face is a small price. I'd rather be early and wrong than late and right.

qa.q: What had caused the burning smell?
qa.a: A burnt fuse in the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel while Wasim teased on the way home?
qa.a: A little embarrassed, with a warm face, but at peace with it, seeing it as a small price to pay.

qa.q: What habit made Suraj's quick exit possible?
qa.a: Finding the two exits before sitting down, so when the staff member asked people to go outside, Suraj knew exactly where to walk.

qa.q: How might Wasim see the evening, having followed Suraj out?
qa.a: Wasim missed three songs and enjoyed the teasing, but was also outside early and safe in case it had been serious.

grounding: A young adult checks exits in advance and follows a staff warning straight away, accepting mild embarrassment when it proves a false alarm.

passage:
Guest note, hill homestay near Madikeri. Yamini Poovaiah, owner.
Vaibhav, 25, checked in on Monday. Within ten minutes he had asked me where the cottage's second exit was and whether there was a torch by the bed. I noticed a small pouch clipped to his daypack: torch, whistle, water, copies of his ID.
On Wednesday afternoon the district issued a landslide advisory for our road and asked visitors to move to town. Most guests stayed on the veranda with their coffee; the rain didn't look like much. Vaibhav packed within twenty minutes. He said, "I'll feel silly if nothing happens, but that's better than being stuck." The others teased him a little.
Nothing happened on our road. On Friday he messaged to thank us and said he'd come back in the dry season.
Since then, I have pinned the district helpline numbers and exit map by every door.

qa.q: What was in the pouch clipped to Vaibhav's daypack?
qa.a: A torch, a whistle, water and copies of his ID.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's remark about feeling silly show about his thinking?
qa.a: He expected possible embarrassment but judged it a small price compared with being stuck, so he acted on the advisory without waiting for proof.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's habits make leaving early easy, and what did Yamini do next?
qa.a: Knowing the exits and keeping a small kit let him pack in twenty minutes; Yamini then pinned helpline numbers and exit maps by every door.

qa.q: How might the guests who teased Vaibhav think about it later?
qa.a: They might feel he overreacted since nothing happened, or quietly wonder what they would have done if the road had gone.

grounding: An adult notes exits, carries a small kit and leaves on an official warning, accepting the risk of a false alarm.

passage:
12 March, Port Blair

The ground swayed around eleven, a long slow roll. Twenty minutes later the official alert came: possible tsunami, move away from the shore to higher ground. Francis, across from me at the seafront café, laughed and ordered another tea. "These come every few months, yaar. Never anything."
I already had my small bag: water, torch, charger, ID copies. Last month I'd walked the route up the hill to the church, so I knew it took twelve minutes. I paid and went. I felt very dramatic walking past everyone still eating.
The alert was withdrawn at two. Nothing came. Francis sent a photo of his third tea: "Survived, hero 🙂"
Yes, I felt stupid for about ten minutes. But stupid is fine. Late isn't. Same thing next time.
Samir

qa.q: How long did Samir's walk up the hill to the church take?
qa.a: It took twelve minutes.

qa.q: How did Samir feel walking past everyone still eating?
qa.a: Samir felt dramatic and a little foolish, but was still more concerned about being late than about looking silly.

qa.q: What did Samir's preparation do well?
qa.a: Having a small bag ready and having walked the route before meant Samir could follow the alert at once, without debating it.

qa.q: How might Francis see Samir's leaving, and what would change if the wave had come?
qa.a: Francis sees it as funny overcaution; if the wave had come, Francis would have been the one caught at the shore while Samir was already safe.

grounding: An adult follows an official tsunami alert at once with a ready kit and known route, preferring embarrassment to being late.
